## Comparison

Both traces follow nearly identical strategies: identify B as the highest-degree node, assign it Red, then propagate constraints through neighbors C, D, E, F, H and onward to A, G, I. Both arrive at valid 3-colorings that are structurally isomorphic—Trace 1 partitions into {B,I}=Red, {A,C,F}=Blue, {D,E,G,H}=Green, while Trace 2 partitions into {B,I}=Red, {A,C,F}=Green, {D,E,G,H}=Blue—just with Blue and Green swapped.

The key divergence is in post-solution branch exploration. Trace 1 briefly tests E=Blue, immediately finds a conflict with C=Blue, and prunes it; the sibling trace never bothers with this branch, confirming it was unnecessary. Trace 2 extensively explores F=Blue, derives a complete second valid solution, then explicitly discards it in favor of the first; the sibling trace never explores this alternative, yet reaches an equally valid answer, showing the branch was unnecessary for correctness.

Both traces suffer from severe verification redundancy. Trace 1 re-checks all 13 edges of the same solution at least four separate times (numbers, then color names, then twice more). Trace 2 similarly re-verifies its first solution after already confirming it. The sibling traces demonstrate that a single verification suffices.

## Trace 1

## Trace 2

⟦CYCLE⟧ trace=2 conf=clear start="Let's explore $C(F) = B$." end="the second one is also fine." basis=The solver opens an alternative branch by setting F=Blue instead of Green, derives a complete valid second solution, then explicitly eliminates it by choosing the first solution. The branch has visible downstream effect: the comparison informs the final output choice.⟦LOOP⟧ trace=2 conf=probable start="Let's check all edges with these colors." end="13. H-I: Blue-Red. OK." basis=Re-verifies all 13 edges of the first solution, which was already fully verified earlier using abbreviated color labels (G-B, G-R, etc.); the re-check adds no new information.
